Rectangle on a Chessboard

InvariantsArithmeticAlgorithms
Game: Cover equal amounts of the light and dark squares of a chessboard with one rectangle.
How to play: Drag the rectangle, pull the corner to resize it, or use the sliders. Watch the two areas.

Look for the math

A rectangle placed on a chessboard may cover equal amounts of the two colours — but only in two very particular situations.

When it works

The page's condition is an if and only if: a rectangle covers equal areas of the two colours exactly when one of its sides is an even whole number of square sides, or its centre lies on a grid line. An even side pairs a light square with a dark one in every strip; a centre on a line gives a matching symmetry.

Why nothing else works

Any rectangle splits into at most three pieces: one with even width, one with even height, and one with both sides less than two. Checking the three small prototype shapes shows that the last piece is unbalanced unless its centre lies on a grid line. A random placement almost surely fails that, so for a rectangle without an even side the probability of balance is zero; with an even side it is one.

The logic test checks the condition on 20,736 placements, the three-piece split on 10,000 more, and the chessboard corollary: rectangles with at least one integer side tile a rectangle with an integer side.

Tick "Show the split". Which of the pieces is the one that decides the answer?
